title: Mastery Challenge: Earth, Weather & Climate
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Earth, Weather & Climate Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Ten questions from across the tree so far: Earth's spheres, minerals, rocks and soil, forecasts, hazard safety and the climate debate. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Earth, Weather & Climate Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Ten questions from across the tree, from a grain of quartz to the forecast on your phone. Level 1 split the planet into four spheres; now see how far that picture reaches. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Earth, Weather & Climate: mastered
learned: How Earth's rock, air, water and life link into one system that shapes weather and climate.
Why a rock's crystals, grains or bands reveal how and where it formed.
How balloons, radar, satellites and physics become the odds in your forecast.
What to do when warnings come, from Drop, Cover and Hold On to Turn Around, Don't Drown.

questions.prompt: Why does the biosphere overlap all of Earth's other spheres?

options.label: It's the largest sphere by mass
options.rationale: It's defined by where life is, not by size.

options.label: Life is found in rock, water and air alike
It sits between the crust and the air
options.rationale: It isn't a layer; it's wherever life exists.

options.label: It includes all of Earth's water
options.rationale: That's the hydrosphere.

questions.explanation: The biosphere is everywhere life exists, so it overlaps the geosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere.

questions.prompt: An unknown mineral leaves a scratch on a glass window. On the Mohs scale, what does that tell you?

options.label: It's softer than glass, below about 5.5
options.rationale: A softer mineral couldn't scratch the glass.

options.label: It must be a diamond, at 10
options.rationale: Anything harder than glass will scratch it, quartz included.

options.label: It's harder than glass, which rates about 5.5
Nothing: the scratch test only ranks metals
options.rationale: The Mohs scale ranks minerals by scratch hardness.

questions.explanation: A harder mineral scratches a softer one, so anything that scratches glass (about 5.5) is harder than glass, like quartz at 7.

questions.prompt: Obsidian is glassy, with no crystals at all. What does that say about how it formed?

options.label: Its lava chilled too fast for crystals to grow
It cooled very slowly, deep underground
options.rationale: Slow cooling grows big crystals.

options.label: It was squeezed flat by heat and pressure
options.rationale: That's how metamorphic foliation forms.

options.label: It was cemented together from loose sand
options.rationale: That's how sandstone forms.

questions.explanation: Obsidian is volcanic glass: lava cooled so fast that no crystals had time to form.

questions.prompt: A typical healthy soil is about 45% mineral matter. What makes up most of the rest?

options.label: Solid bedrock, mixed evenly through it
options.rationale: Bedrock lies below the soil and isn't soil.

options.label: Organic matter, about half the soil
options.rationale: Organic matter is only about 5%.

options.label: Pure quartz sand, no matter where
options.rationale: Sand is part of the mineral matter.

options.label: Water and air, about a quarter each

questions.explanation: A typical healthy soil is about 45% minerals, 25% water, 25% air and 5% organic matter.

questions.prompt: What does a radiosonde radio back to the ground every second as its balloon climbs?

options.label: Air pressure, temperature, humidity and its position
Photos of the clouds below it
options.rationale: Satellites take the pictures.

options.label: The speed of raindrops toward it
options.rationale: That's what Doppler radar measures.

options.label: Tomorrow's forecast for its launch site
options.rationale: Forecasts come from models, not balloons.

questions.explanation: A radiosonde reports pressure, temperature, relative humidity and GPS position each second; its tracked position gives the winds.

questions.prompt: Why do forecasters run the same model many times from slightly different starting points?

options.label: To use up spare time on the supercomputer
options.rationale: The runs have a real purpose.

options.label: Because each run uses a different planet's physics
options.rationale: The physics is the same; the starting points differ.

options.label: To see how small errors grow and turn that into odds
To wait until one run matches yesterday's weather
options.rationale: They're forecasting the future, not the past.

questions.explanation: Small errors in the starting picture grow in a chaotic atmosphere, so the spread of many runs becomes a probability.

questions.prompt: Your phone shows a Flash Flood Warning for your area. What does it mean, and what should you do if you're in a flood-prone spot?

options.label: Flooding is possible later, so review your plans
options.rationale: That describes a watch.

options.label: A flash flood is imminent or happening: go to high ground
Flooding has ended, so roads are safe again
options.rationale: A warning means the danger is here now.

options.label: Heavy rain is likely next week, so buy supplies
options.rationale: Warnings are for immediate danger.

questions.explanation: A flash flood warning means a flash flood is imminent or occurring; in a flood-prone area, move to high ground right away.

questions.prompt: A viral post says a major quake will strike your city next Friday. Why should you doubt it?

options.label: Quakes only happen on weekends
options.rationale: Quakes can strike on any day.

options.label: Quakes are too small to predict
options.rationale: Size isn't the issue; timing is.

options.label: Only volcanoes can be predicted, never quakes
options.rationale: Volcano alerts are a different system.

options.label: No one has ever predicted a major quake's date, place and size

questions.explanation: No scientist has ever predicted a major earthquake's date and time, location and magnitude; scientists give probabilities instead.

questions.prompt: In a heat wave, why does a city often stay hot long after sunset?

options.label: Streetlights heat the air all night
options.rationale: The stored heat comes from the Sun.

options.label: Its roofs and roads slowly give back stored heat
Cities are always closer to the Equator
options.rationale: Heat islands form in cities everywhere.

options.label: City air holds no water vapor at all
options.rationale: Humidity isn't what keeps city nights hot.

questions.explanation: Roofs, roads and parking lots absorb the Sun's heat and release it slowly, so US cities run about 2 to 5°F warmer at night.

questions.prompt: Which pair best sums up the main arguments for and against carbon pricing?

options.label: For: it's cost-effective. Against: it weighs more on lower-income homes
For: it ends all emissions at once. Against: it's illegal
options.rationale: Neither is the argument either side makes.

options.label: For: it cools the planet quickly. Against: it harms ozone
options.rationale: Those points are about solar geoengineering.

options.label: For: no CO2 while running. Against: long-lived waste
options.rationale: Those points are about nuclear power.

questions.explanation: Supporters call carbon pricing a cost-effective way to cut emissions; critics say higher energy costs hit lower-income households harder.
